evidence.claim: An emigrant road winds past the waterworks of gold mining.
evidence.quote: You can see signs of this road on either side of Highway 20 as it winds along Washington Ridge.

evidence.claim: An emigrant road winds past the waterworks of gold mining.
evidence.quote: It is one of many ditches built by the South Yuba Canal Company to carry water to Nevada County gold mines.

evidence.claim: East of Nevada City, Highway 20 climbs as a two-lane road along Harmony Ridge and Washington Ridge.
evidence.quote: SR 20 resumes its eastward course as a two-lane highway. The roadway climbs from Nevada City and follows Harmony Ridge and Washington Ridge

evidence.claim: A stretch near its eastern end belongs to California’s State Scenic Highway System and the larger Yuba-Donner National Forest Scenic Byway.
evidence.quote: has been designated as such for 6 miles (9.7 km) near the east end; this is part of the federally designated Yuba-Donner Scenic Byway, a National Forest Scenic Byway

evidence.claim: The Forest Service presents the drive between Nevada City and Interstate 80 as a route for hiking, biking and camping, with traces of the 1850 Emigrant Trail cutoff along the way.
evidence.quote: Travel Highway 20 between Nevada City and Interstate 80 for hiking, biking and camping opportunities. Along the way, spot traces of the 1850 cutoff of the Emigrant Trail as it winds along Washington Ridge.

evidence.claim: Between Nevada City and Bear Valley, the highway largely follows that cutoff.
evidence.quote: Highway 20 between Bear Valley and Nevada City largely follows the trace of the 1850 cutoff of the Emigrant Trail.

evidence.claim: It became a toll road and then a public turnpike, retaining the name Old Emigrant Road.
evidence.quote: Although it later became a toll road, and later a public turnpike, it was still referred to as the Old Emigrant Road.

evidence.claim: Sections of the Pioneer Trail now follow its trace; signs of the earlier road remain on both sides of Highway 20.
evidence.quote: You can see signs of this road on either side of Highway 20 as it winds along Washington Ridge. Pioneer Trail sections follow the trace of the old Emigrant road.

evidence.claim: The state highway extension reached Emigrant Gap in 1919 as part of the Tahoe-Ukiah Highway. The numbered Sign Route 20 followed in 1934.
evidence.quote: This state highway was significantly extended in both directions in 1919, west to Ukiah and east to Emigrant Gap, creating what was known as the Tahoe-Ukiah Highway

evidence.claim: The state highway extension reached Emigrant Gap in 1919 as part of the Tahoe-Ukiah Highway. The numbered Sign Route 20 followed in 1934.
evidence.quote: became Sign Route 20 in 1934

evidence.claim: Traveling east, Skillman Flat introduces the mining country through a different kind of channel: the Ridge Ditch, built in 1857–58 to carry water to gold mines.
evidence.quote: Skillman Flat is the site of a lumber mill that burned down in 1858. The trail here follows the Ridge Ditch, constructed in 1857-58. It is one of many ditches built by the South Yuba Canal Company to carry water to Nevada County gold mines.

evidence.claim: Farther along, Omega Overlook gives a view of the Alpha and Omega Diggins.
evidence.quote: Omega Overlook. From the overlook one can see the Alpha and Omega Diggins

evidence.claim: Continuing beyond the ridge country, the broader highway descends through hairpin turns into Bear Valley before climbing toward I-80.
evidence.quote: before descending into the Bear Valley via a series of hairpin turns, and then climbing, just north of Emigrant Gap, to its end at I-80 at Yuba Pass.

evidence.claim: At Skillman Flat, the Pioneer Trail follows the Ridge Ditch, a water channel built in 1857–58 by the South Yuba Canal Company for Nevada County’s gold mines.
evidence.quote: Skillman Flat is the site of a lumber mill that burned down in 1858. The trail here follows the Ridge Ditch, constructed in 1857-58. It is one of many ditches built by the South Yuba Canal Company to carry water to Nevada County gold mines.

evidence.claim: The flat was also a lumber-mill site. Skillman’s mill burned in 1858, losing 300,000 feet of lumber.
evidence.quote: Skillman Flat is the site of a lumber mill that burned down in 1858.

evidence.claim: The flat was also a lumber-mill site. Skillman’s mill burned in 1858, losing 300,000 feet of lumber.
evidence.quote: Skillman's was located about 1 mile west of Alpha and burned in 1858 with a loss of 300,000 feet of lumber.

evidence.claim: Lumber from the local sawmills supplied Alpha’s buildings, giving the mining town wooden structures in place of the canvas buildings common in other gold-rush settlements.
evidence.quote: The sawmills provided Alpha with a readily source of lumber for home building which meant that unlike many gold rush towns, it was not full of canvas stores and buildings.

evidence.claim: The mill stood about one mile west of Alpha, where at least three sawmills operated in the 1850s. Whether Skillman’s was rebuilt is unclear.
evidence.quote: In the 1850s, it had at least three sawmills: McWorthey's, Skillman's and Murdock's.  Skillman's was located about 1 mile west of Alpha and burned in 1858 with a loss of 300,000 feet of lumber. Murdock's mill burned in 1859. It is not clear whether either mill was rebuilt.

evidence.claim: Water shortages once set the rhythm of mining at Alpha: the settlement was busy in winter and largely deserted in summer.
evidence.quote: An early problem was a scarcity of water during the summer. This meant that the area was busy and populated during the winter but largely deserted during the summer.

evidence.claim: Ditches began to change that pattern. In January 1858, the South Yuba Canal brought a substantial supply through flumes and ditches, and hydraulic mining expanded.
evidence.quote: Finally, in January 1858, the South Yuba Canal arrived, bringing a substantial supply of water through an extensive and expensive series of flumes and ditches. With a reliable source of water, hydraulic mining soon blossomed.

evidence.claim: The mines depleted quickly. By the mid-1860s, only Captain Merriman’s mine remained in operation.
evidence.quote: However, the mines quickly became depleted and by the mid-1860s, only Captain Merriman's mine was still operating.

evidence.claim: As residents left, empty buildings became firewood or building material for neighboring Omega.
evidence.quote: Gradually, empty buildings were torn down and they would be used for firewood or to build in Omega.

evidence.claim: Many residents moved to Omega as Alpha declined. The Masonic lodge moved there too, while other residents left to follow new strikes in Nevada.
evidence.quote: Many residents moved one mile east to Omega, which continued to flourish for many years. The Masonic Lodge was moved to Omega. Other residents followed new strikes in Nevada.

evidence.claim: The Alpha and Omega Diggins are visible from Omega Overlook.
evidence.quote: From the overlook one can see the Alpha and Omega Diggins

evidence.claim: Their water supply involved more than a ditch beside the road: water diverted from the Yuba River entered the Omega Ditch and wooden flumes suspended from granite cliffs above the river.
evidence.quote: Yuba River water was diverted to the Omega Ditch and into wood flumes hung from granite cliffs above the Yuba River.

evidence.claim: The older travel route is close by, too. Fifty yards beyond the historic marker lies a trace of the Old Emigrant Road.
evidence.quote: Fifty yards beyond the historic marker you’ll find the trace of the Old Emigrant Road.

evidence.claim: The Pioneer Trail follows that trace east to Diamond Creek Road, one and a half miles away.
evidence.quote: The Pioneer Trail follows it to the Diamond Creek Road, one and one half miles east.

evidence.claim: The state landmark inscription records that hydraulic excavations engulfed most of the original townsites of Alpha and Omega.
evidence.quote: The tremendous hydraulic diggings, visible from near this point, engulfed most of the original townsites.
